abstract.p: The development of the Nusantara Capital City (IKN) in Indonesia has spurred economic transformation amidst environmental pressures arising from changes in land use, industrial activity and infrastructure expansion in the surrounding areas. These challenges underscore the crucial importance of environmental management, not only as a consequence of development, but also as a strategic pillar that influences how regional economic activities contribute to the well-being of the community. This study aims to examine environmental quality (EQ) and public prosperity (PP) by analysing the factors that influence them, including the manufacturing sector (MS), infrastructure costs (IC), and labour market performance (LMP). Secondary data were collected from government publications, covering a longitudinal observation period from 2012 to 2024. The research focuses on two areas within the IKN, namely Penajam Paser Utara (PPU) and Kutai Kartanegara (Kukar). A moderation–mediation regression method was applied to test the partial, moderation, and mediation effects among the variables analysed. The empirical findings highlight two important points. First, in the case of PPU, MS is significantly associated with EQ. IC and LMP each have a significant partial effect on PP. Variables such as MS and IC, when moderated by EQ, have a significant impact on PP. Also, IC and LMP, when mediated by EQ, are significantly related to PP. Second, in the case of Kukar, MS has a significant partial effect on both EQ and PP. Moreover, IC shows a significant association with EQ, while LMP significantly increases PP. MS, when moderated by EQ, has a significant effect on PP. Additional evidence indicates that LMP, both moderated and mediated by EQ, shows a significant association with PP. The results of the study offer valuable insights for stakeholders when assessing and considering policy strategies related to PP, while also refreshing knowledge in the economic, social, and environmental fields for scholars. The advantage of this study, which is uncommon in much of the existing literature, lies in the location observed—in this case, the new capital city. In addition to this, the analysis does not focus solely on macroeconomic variables as determinants of PP, but also considers other factors, namely the quality of the environment, both directly and indirectly, in influencing the sustainability of PP.

sec.title: 1.1. Background
sec.p: Althalets et al. [1] and Kuleh et al. [2] argue that the relocation of Indonesia’s administrative centre from Jakarta to the Nusantara Capital City (IKN) in East Kalimantan is driven by several strategic objectives. These include the equitable distribution of development, which has been overly concentrated in one area; accelerating the national economic transformation in line with Indonesia’s vision for 2045; and reducing the burden on Jakarta, which faces risks such as flooding, land subsidence, pollution, and high population density. From a regulatory perspective, Law No. 3 of 2022 on IKN designates the development of the IKN as a national priority, positioning it as a future driver of Indonesia’s economy, a sustainable city on the global stage, and a symbol of national identity that reflects the nation’s diversity. This is grounded in normative, constitutional, and ideological foundations, namely the 1945 Constitution and Pancasila, which underpin and are incorporated into the IKN regulations. These regulations also govern the special authority of the IKN, emphasise the primary benefits of the relocation, establish the legal basis for its gradual implementation, and outline the master plan for the development of the IKN [3].

From a global perspective and in recent scientific works, the relocation of the national capital is also regarded as a policy aimed at redistributing economic growth from the Java-centric region to other parts of Indonesia, such as East Kalimantan. This relocation is intended to support more sustainable development. Khairunnisa [4] emphasises the urgency of this move as part of a more dynamic national scheme, referring to the legality of the system and encompassing dimensions of development governance and economic equality simultaneously. However, this process also presents administrative challenges that must be addressed in accordance with the principles of good governance. Regarding the structural shift involved in the IKN relocation, this reflects how regulations related to the IKN can be constructively understood in terms of the relocation’s targets and their future implications.

Geographically, the IKN is situated in an area encompassing parts of two regions within East Kalimantan Province: Samboja Subdistrict in Kutai Kartanegara (Kukar) and Sepaku Subdistrict in Penajam Paser Utara (PPU). The IKN covers a total area of approximately 256,142 hectares, comprising land taken from both regencies to establish a unified centre of government. This centre serves not only administrative functions but also operates as a distinct core territorial entity, independent of the East Kalimantan Provincial Government, and is known as the IKN Authority. At the planning stage, the development area of the IKN in both regions also represents a new administrative location strategy within a single project.

The relocation of the national capital is systematically linked to efforts to promote prosperity through equitable development and to ultimately open up new economic opportunities, although it remains a subject of debate with mixed consequences. Recent papers predict that this relocation will increase regional economic growth, particularly in East Kalimantan, thereby enabling a substantial rise in regional income and economic output. This could create space for more extensive economic growth than previously experienced, potentially having a vital impact on the prosperity of both local and migrant communities if supported by conducive policies [5]. Conversely, Oktavia et al. [6] observe that the development of the IKN has the potential to generate new jobs, boost income through the involvement of local communities in the development value chain, foster the growth of small and medium enterprises (SMEs), and increase demand for labour and services—all of which are crucial mechanisms for driving the economic prosperity of communities surrounding the IKN. Nevertheless, international literature also emphasises that the added value of relocation to prosperity is highly dependent on the readiness of local human resources, the quality of policy implementation, and the mitigation of environmental and social impacts. This indicates that the relocation of the national capital is not an automatic guarantee of prosperity unless it is balanced with careful planning and implementation in the field, consistent with the principle of quality equity [7].

Besides to administrative and economic implications, the IKN development project also gives rise to various environmental consequences that warrant serious attention. The development of a new, large-scale administrative centre has the potential to trigger changes in land use, increased demand for infrastructure, urban sprawl, and the growth of economic activity (particularly industrial activity), all of which can have a massive impact on environmental conditions [8]. Several recent articles have highlighted that the development of new areas, if not balanced by adequate environmental governance, can give rise to new problems, such as ecosystem fragmentation, increased emissions, a reduction in vegetation cover, water quality degradation, and a decline in environmental carrying capacity [9], [10]. Ultimately, the success of the IKN’s development must be assessed not only economic achievements and public prosperity (PP), but also its capacity to safeguard environmental quality (EQ) in an inclusive manner.

The relationships between the manufacturing industry, infrastructure, employment, the environment, and prosperity require a comprehensive review amid the rapid development of the IKN project. This development is not merely an administrative relocation but holds cross-sectoral significance that determines the success of sustainable development, particularly in terms of prosperity. Hilal et al. [11] emphasise that the relocation of the IKN entails complex economic, environmental, and social implications, including the expansion of sustainable infrastructure, shifts in economic patterns, the growth of new industries, job creation, and environmental impacts such as carbon emissions, urbanisation, and land use. All these factors are interrelated and structurally influence the distribution of prosperity in both the former capital and the new administrative region. Several journals have analysed the impact of the new IKN, which has the potential to foster more equitable regional economic growth through job opportunities and increased income, but simultaneously highlight the risks of land use conflicts, ecosystem damage, and social inclusion issues if planning does not consider all elements of development in an integrated manner [5], [12], [13]. These phenomena underscore the urgent need for cross-disciplinary approaches to guide integrated and equitable policies. More importantly, environmental sustainability in the development of the IKN depends not only on economic performance, but also on ecological monitoring systems, the effectiveness of environmental governance, and the capacity of public institutions to mitigate environmental risks associated with industrial expansion, land-use change and infrastructure development.

sec.title: 1.2. Objectivity and contributions
sec.p: This study focuses on EQ as the key variable in assessing the sustainability of development in the IKN region. Explicitly, the study is designed to unpack the links between the manufacturing sector (MS), infrastructure costs (IC) and labour market performance (LMP) in relation to EQ, whilst highlighting how EQ relates to community prosperity, both directly and indirectly. By placing EQ at the centre of the investigation, this study seeks to identify the environmental consequences of IKN development and their implications for the sustainability of community well-being.

By discovering the relationship between EQ and PP, as well as the variables influencing them, this research is expected to be considered by both academic and policy-making communities. Firstly, quantitative investigations, both direct and indirect, can enrich academic knowledge, enabling other scientists to conduct studies on related topics. Secondly, the study’s findings provide an evaluation tool for the government to formulate rational policies that not only focus on improvements in manufacturing, infrastructure, and employment sectors to foster prosperity but also take into account environmental considerations. The paper is structured into six chapters. Section One (Introduction) presents the background, objectives, and contributions of the research. Section Two (Literature Review) outlines the fundamental theory, empirical basis, research gap and study contribution, as well as conceptual framework. Section Three (Methodology) details the approach, data description, and analytical methods. Section Four (Empirical Findings) reports the research results and discusses their implications, supported by comparisons with relevant literature. Section Five (Conclusion) summarises the research findings, addresses the study's limitations for consideration in future research, and offers practical recommendations for policymakers.

sec.title: 2.1. Fundamental theory
sec.p: The fundamental theory underpinning this study is rooted on EQ and PP, which are influenced by macroeconomic factors such as the MS, IC, and LMP. In development economics, macroeconomic variables like industrial structure play a crucial role in driving productivity growth and increases in per capita income. The MS is generally regarded as one of the main drivers of economic growth, as it is capable of boosting productivity, optimising value added for the economy, and creating jobs. Through the expansion of labour absorption and production activities, the development of the MS has the potential to contribute to income inclusivity and regional prosperity. However, these benefits must be balanced with strategic environmental management to ensure that the resulting economic growth remains consistent with the principles of sustainable development [14], [15], [16], [17], [18], [19].

Infrastructure function, LMP, and EQ converge within the framework of community prosperity through the interaction between quality of life and economic growth. Adequate infrastructure not only accelerates the mobility of goods and services but also broadens community access to essential public services and the labour market, thereby leading to increased prosperity and income. Investment in human capital, employment, and infrastructure can enhance the quality of social services, create new job opportunities, and reduce transaction costs. Moreover, the environment is a fundamental attribute in determining long-term prosperity, as a healthy environment improves quality of life, effectively reducing public health costs and enabling sustainable economic activity. The contemporary macroeconomic framework addresses the causality between economic outcomes and the environmental resource paradox, whereby misaligned development can diminish community prosperity and degrade EQ [20], [21], [22], [23].

sec.title: 2.2. Empirical basis
sec.p: The empirical basis of this study focuses on the relationship between the MS, IC, and LMP in relation to EQ. Besides, it navigates how the MS, IC, LMP, and EQ collectively influence PP. Additionally, the study investigates the impact of the MS, IC, and LMP on PP mediated by EQ. The relationships between these variables are established through the replication of previous articles.

Various academic works have concluded that the MS, LMP and infrastructure development form the backbone of social prosperity and economic growth. Industrial activity and infrastructure investment can make a positive contribution to employment opportunities, strengthen economic capacity and boost regional productivity. On the one hand, these economic benefits are often accompanied by consequences that vary depending on the development governance framework in place, such as EQ [24], [25].

To exacerbate the situation, infrastructure and industrial growth without clear planning can place significant pressure on the environment, thereby undermining long-term prosperity and residents’ quality of life. Qian [26] found that high-intensity industrialisation and infrastructure investment can increase environmental degradation and pollution in Indonesia, China, and India if not accompanied by robust ecological management policies, thus complicating efforts to achieve sustainable development. A manuscript on the multidimensional linearity between economic development and EQ demonstrates that, after reaching a certain threshold of green technology advancement and per capita income, most more sustainable or developed countries tend to reduce negative environmental impacts while continuing to strengthen their economic performance [27]. This is also evident in Slovakia, where the adoption of environmentally friendly clean technology innovations highlights the urgency of green growth for sustainable prosperity, which depends not only on economic value but also on the integration of industrial development, the labour market, infrastructure, and environmental protection through consistent policies [28].

Machado et al. [29] demonstrate that when the MS adopts sustainable production methods—such as waste reduction and energy efficiency—it not only stimulates economic activity but also mitigates environmental impacts through more efficient resource management. Moreover, it supports long-term prosperity. Essentially, sustainable manufacturing emphasises the integration of industrial technology with environmentally friendly practices as a means of revitalising industrial growth towards more environmentally conscious and controlled economic development. Robust infrastructure—including energy, communication networks, and transportation—facilitates market access and enhances industrial productivity, thereby strengthening the link between manufacturing output and employment opportunities. Specifically, the developing economies of many European Union (EU) countries suggest that holistic infrastructure development can enhance sustainable growth by expanding the workforce and fostering technological innovation, which ultimately accelerates economic growth while promoting the prosperity of the population [30]. In the context of sustainability, the labour market cycle is evolving as employability and competence become increasingly complex, enabling the workforce to support the green economy without compromising EQ.

To date, the interconnection between labour, industry, and EQ in achieving sustainable prosperity has been the focus of considerable attention from scholars and various communities [31], [32], [33]. The relationship between the manufacturing industry, the labour market, and prosperity cannot be considered independently of the environmental context. For example, increased investment in industrial clusters, accompanied by expanding employment opportunities and improved infrastructure quality in Taiwan, routinely has a significant impact on economic output. Nonetheless, it also causes environmental changes if not underpinned by sustainability principles [34], [35]. The Ecological Modernisation Theory framework, including the Porter Hypothesis, has been applied in cases in China, countries within the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), and several other nations. In these contexts, effective environmental regulations can stimulate cleaner industrial innovation, thereby collectively enhancing productivity, increasing social prosperity, and creating new jobs without degrading EQ [36], [37], [38].

sec.title: 2.3. Research gap and study contribution
sec.p: Although the links between industrialisation, the labour market, infrastructure development, EQ and community prosperity have been extensively discussed in the literature on regional development, the majority of cross-case studies tend to examine these links in isolation [39]. Much research is more fragmented in its focus on the economic impacts of development on regional growth, whilst EQ is often positioned as a risk to development rather than as a variable that helps determine the sustainability of community prosperity. At the same time, various studies on new town development, urban expansion and urbanisation often prove that the success of regional development is determined not only by economic growth, but also by the capacity for ecological governance and the continuous maintenance of EQ.

In the scope of the relocation of the national capital, some recent studies have focused primarily on policy implications, urban sprawl, changes in land use, spatial planning, and the environmental impacts of developing new areas [40], [41]. However, specifically, there is still relatively little evidence identifying the relationship between the MS, LMP, IC, EQ, and community prosperity in the capital’s buffer zones. This limitation is evident in the literature on the IKN in East Kalimantan Province, which focuses solely on aspects of development planning, macroeconomic projections, or governance; consequently, the dynamics of development in key buffer zones such as PPU Regency and Kukar Regency have yet to be evaluated quantitatively to any significant extent.

Another research gap lies in the role of EQ within the analytical model. Some of the literature reviewed treats EQ as a standalone independent or dependent variable [41], [42], [43]. In contrast, this study views EQ as a more complex axis: not only is it directly linked to community well-being, but it is also positioned as a moderating and mediating variable in the relationship between the MS, IC, LMP, and community well-being. By comparing two regional areas collectively, this study is expected to provide fresh insights into how economic development and EQ interact to influence PP in regions undergoing macro-level growth and development transformation.

International literature over the past five years has also noted that the development of urban areas and large-scale new capital cities is increasingly viewed as an issue that relates not only to economic growth, but also to regional governance and environmental sustainability. In practice, this is illustrated in cross-case studies where urban expansion, land-use changes and infrastructure development often place pressure on EQ, thereby necessitating the implementation of environmental impact assessments with practical ecological governance [44], [45], [46]. At the same time, the success of new area development is no longer assessed solely through economic benchmarks, but also through the government’s ability to maintain a balance between regional growth, the quality of life of the community, and ecosystem conservation. In Indonesia itself, papers on the development of the IKN have also begun to highlight the importance of smart, sustainable urban development, environmental management and integrated urban governance as critical phases for sustainable development [47], [48]. Besides, some of these studies still focus on aspects of planning, governance and spatial planning, or general environmental implications, whilst there is still little empirical research examining the interrelationships between the MS, IC, LMP, EQ and community prosperity in the IKN’s buffer zones. It is this situation that forms one of the contexts for the development of the model in this study.

sec.title: 2.4. Conceptual framework
sec.p: Figure 1 visualises the conceptual framework. The five identified variables are: (1) the MS, (2) IC, (3) LMP, (4) EQ, and (5) PP. The MS, LMP, and IC serve as independent variables, while PP functions as the dependent variable. In addition, EQ plays a multifaceted role, modulating the relationships within the framework. In direct relationships, it acts as both an independent and dependent variable; in indirect relationships, it serves as a moderating and mediating variable.
Referring to the conceptual framework outlined above, which is reflected in the basic theory and empirical evidence presented, thirteen hypotheses are proposed as follows:
H1–H3: The MS, IC, and LMP are negatively associated with EQ.
H4–H7: The MS, IC, LMP, and EQ are positively associated with PP.
H8–H10: The MS, IC, and LMP, moderated by EQ, are associated with PP.
H11–H13: The MS, IC, and LMP, as mediated by EQ are associated with PP.

sec.title: 3.1. Approach
sec.p: The associative-verificative approach was selected to examine the relationships among two or more variables. In this instance, the approach was employed to test the validity of existing hypotheses or theories using empirical data. The relationships among the MS, IC, LMP, EQ, and PP were quantitatively estimated using statistical methods. The research sample was drawn from two districts adjacent to the IKN, namely PPU and Kukar.

sec.title: 3.2. Data description
sec.p: Secondary data were obtained from annual reports provided by external sources, specifically government agencies. These data are longitudinal, covering two buffer zones of the IKN over the period from 2012 to 2024. Data collection was conducted using documentary techniques. The dataset comprises variables related to the MS, IC, LMP, EQ, and PP. In total, five variables were dissected. The operational definitions of each variable are presented in Table 1. As this study utilises annual data for the period 2012 to 2024 across two regions—PPU Regency and Kukar Regency—the raw observations for each region cover thirteen years, corresponding to the number of years of observation. This number of observations corresponds to the availability of annual data released by official government bodies and accessible to the public. All variables were tabulated based on annual data without converting the data into monthly or quarterly figures. An explanation of the number of observations applied to each regression model is presented in the empirical evidence section to aid in the interpretation of the estimation results. Regression models were calculated separately for PPU and Kukar.

sec.p: Operationally, the LMP variable relies on the Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR) parameter. This indicator measures the proportion of the working-age population (15 years and older) that participates in the labour force within a given region over a specific period. It is calculated by dividing the total labour force by the entire working-age population and multiplying the result by 100, yielding a value expressed as a percentage (%). The labour force comprises individuals who are employed—including those temporarily not working—as well as those who are unemployed, including individuals actively seeking employment. According to the classification used by BPS, the unemployed category also encompasses individuals preparing to start a business, those who have ceased searching for work due to a perceived lack of job opportunities, and individuals who have secured employment but have yet to begin working. In short, the LFPR indicates the intensity of labour force participation; it is not a direct measure of job creation, job quality, or labour absorption, as these specific labour market dimensions are not examined separately within the scope of this study.

The IKLH is an environmental indicator comprising three components: air quality (emissions, pollution, and population density), water quality (river cleanliness, domestic and industrial waste), and land quality (availability of green spaces and forest degradation). The IKLH has only been calculated and published regularly at the city and district levels since around 2020 by the Ministry of Environment and Forestry (KLHK); therefore, figures for previous years are either unavailable or have not been officially calculated for many regions, including PPU and Kukar. Since 2020, the IKLH value has been a composite of four components: the Water Quality Index (IKA), Air Quality Index (IKU), Land Quality Index (IKL), and Marine Water Quality Index (IKAL). Under the Regulation of the KLHK Number 27 of 2021, the formula and weighting for the Environmental Quality Index (IKLH) vary according to the administrative level [56]. At the regency and city level, the IKLH is estimated based on the IKA (37.6%), IKU (40.5%), and IKL (21.9%), excluding the IKAL. Regarding its components, the IKA assesses water quality based on parameters such as pH, chemical oxygen demand (COD), biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), dissolved oxygen (DO), total suspended solids (TSS), nitrates, total nitrogen, total phosphates, chlorophyll-a, fecal coliform bacteria, and transparency. The IKU is quantified based on the concentrations of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide, while the IKL relies on metrics concerning non-forest vegetation, the quality of forest cover, and peat ecosystems. At the provincial and national levels, the IKLH formula comprises the IKA (34%), IKU (42.8%), IKL (13.3%), and IKAL (9.9%)—the latter of which measures marine water quality through parameters including TSS, total ammonia, oil and grease, DO, and orthophosphates [57], [58]. These variations in the formula reflect differences in the units of calculation: the IKLH for regencies/cities is assessed based on environmental components specific to each administrative territory, whereas the provincial IKLH is derived by aggregating the average values of these components from all regencies/cities within that province. Methodologically, at the national level, the IKLH components are aggregated from the provincial level by compiling the coefficients from each province; consequently, the composition and weighting of the IKLH components at the provincial and national scales cannot be equated with the formula used at the regency/city level.

Within the modelling framework, the IKLH variable is designed as a proxy for the environmental impact of regional development, as it represents the state of water quality, soil quality, air quality and aquatic EQ. Changes in the IKLH value state the environmental consequences arising from changes in land use, infrastructure development, urban expansion, growing population pressure, or increased industrial activity throughout the course of the IKN’s development. In essence, the IKLH is considered relevant for examining the link between economic development and environmental sustainability within the IKN’s buffer zone.

For the record, the IKLH data is a composite indicator used by the KLHK to assess the environmental condition of a region. Before 2020, the IKLH was calculated based on three main components, namely IKA, IKU and IKL. The availability of IKLH data at the district/city level is also a crucial factor in this study. Official IKLH data for PPU Regency and Kukar Regency have not been consistently published by the KLHK across the entire observation period. Given the limitations in certain periods when regency-level IKLH data were unavailable, this study utilised the IKLH values for East Kalimantan Province, published online, as a reference value to maintain the continuity of longitudinal data. Therefore, there are several years of observation in which the IKLH values for both PPU and Kukar are identical, as they are based on the same provincial reference source. Once IKLH data at regency level became available, the values were analysed separately for each regency, as released by the relevant authorities. According to the KLHK’s regulations, there are five categories in the IKLH based on a region’s ecosystem typology [56]. Firstly, ‘very good’ (score 90–100), indicating a highly natural, healthy environment with minimal pollution. Secondly, ‘good’ (score 70–89), where the environment is in a healthy condition and there is little impact from human activity, yet the ecosystem functions optimally. Third, ‘moderate’ (score 50–69), where the environment is beginning to come under pressure and is experiencing mild pollution due to industrial or domestic activities. Fourth, ‘poor’ (score 25–49), where EQ is poor and there is significant pollution and ecosystem damage. Fifth, ‘very poor’ (score 0–24), an environmental condition classified as heavily polluted, thereby posing a risk to health. To enhance transparency and facilitate the replication of the study, all IKLH data—including observations for the period using time frames and provincial reference values from official data provided by various government agencies—are presented in the appendix at the end of this paper.

sec.p: An autocorrelation test was applied using the D–W statistic to determine whether or not there was autocorrelation in the residuals across observation periods. In this context, a D–W value close to 2 indicates the absence of autocorrelation in the regression model. A D–W value close to 0 indicates the presence of positive autocorrelation, whilst a value close to 4 reflects the presence of negative autocorrelation. Indeed, the closer the D–W value is to 2, the better the assumption of residual independence in the regression model is satisfied.

caption.title: Results of the autocorrelation tests for both regional cases

sec.p: Referring to Table 8 about the results of the autocorrelation tests for both regional cases, where the D–W values across all models fall within the range of 0 to 2, with varying degrees of proximity to the ideal value of 2. There appears to be a difference in the level of residual independence between models depending on the study region. Firstly, in the EQ model, the D–W value in PPU is 0.922, suggesting a tendency towards positive autocorrelation in the residuals. Conversely, in the Kukar case, the D–W value reaches 1.936, very close to the ideal value of 2; it can thus be concluded that the residuals in the EQ model are relatively more independent. Furthermore, in the PP model, the D–W value in PPU was 1.455 and in Kukar it was 1.207. Both values remain below 2, but the PP model in PPU indicates a higher level of residual independence compared to the PP model in Kukar. Overall, the EQ model in Kukar is the one with the D–W value closest to the ideal condition, whilst the EQ model in PPU indicates a relatively stronger positive autocorrelation.

In the first model, for example, the Tolerance values range from 0.695 to 0.852, whilst the VIF values range from 1.174 to 1.438. sec.p: The results of the multicollinearity test for the Kukar case also show a similar pattern. In the first model, the Tolerance values ranged from 0.941 to 0.976 and the VIF values from 1.024 to 1.063. Referring to Table 10, it is concluded that there is no statistical evidence to suggest the presence of multicollinearity that could potentially disrupt the stability of the regression coefficient estimates; therefore, all independent variables remain suitable for inclusion in the empirical model.

sec.title: 5. Discussion
sec.p: Although PPU Regency and Kukar Regency are two buffer zones that are both part of the IKN development system, empirical evidence actually reveals varying patterns of statistical relationships between the two regions. These quite striking differences suggest that the development characteristics of each region have the potential to produce non-uniform responses to the dynamics of the MS, IC, the labour market, EQ, and community prosperity [69]. Dou and Guan [70] report that heterogeneity in regional characteristics, economic structure, institutional capacity and the quality of environmental governance can cause the relationships between development variables to behave differently in each region; consequently, existing findings cannot be assumed to be uniform across regions. Additionally, the interpretation of study results must begin with an understanding of the characteristics of each region before drawing policy implications. Through this approach, the resulting policy directions will be better accommodated and remain within the bounds supported by the statistical relationships identified in each observation [69], [71].

The investigation in PPU reveals that the MS has a positive and significant relationship with EQ, whereas IC and LMP show a negative but statistically insignificant relationship. In the equation for PP, variables such as IC and LMP exhibit a positive and significant relationship with PP, while the coefficients for the MS and EQ are not significant. Interaction terms between the MS and EQ, as well as between IC and EQ, indicate a positive and significant relationship with PP. Conversely, the interaction term between LMP and EQ does not show a significant relationship. Regarding mediation, the indirect effects of IC and LMP on PP—mediated through EQ—are positive and significant; however, the indirect effect of the MS on PP through EQ is not statistically significant.

Nowadays, growth in the MS often has a dual impact on EQ and PP [72]. On the one hand, circulation in manufacturing can serve as a catalyst for improving EQ by promoting environmentally friendly production management through the adoption of clean technologies, thereby contributing positively to the quality of life in surrounding communities. For example, in China’s manufacturing industry, enhanced environmental performance can create a synergistic relationship between employment opportunities and economic benefits, particularly when companies implement green technological innovations that foster output growth and job stability without harming the environment [73]. From another perspective, there are clear trade-offs: large IC combined with a low-skill-oriented labour market and high labour intensity generally lead to a decline in EQ due to excessive energy consumption and emissions. This is exemplified by Ağazade’s [74] study on the fragile environmental pillar in many OECD countries. Traditional industrial approaches that are destructive in the short term can also accelerate environmental degradation while incurring social costs such as expensive infrastructure and pollution prevention measures, which place pressure on community welfare.

Global empirical evidence, including examples from China, shows that the causality between industrial growth, EQ, and population welfare are strongly influenced by industrial structure, environmental policy, and labour market characteristics [75], [76], [77]. Porter’s theory posits that changes in environmental regulations can drive corporate efficiency and innovation, thereby balancing manufacturing output by minimising ecological impacts and massively increasing welfare. On the contrary, if regulations are less stringent—in accordance with the Pollution Haven Hypothesis—companies may choose production locations with lax environmental policies to reduce costs, thereby compromising local welfare and EQ. Although physical infrastructure that initially increases labour mobility, social access, and cost savings is considered a breakthrough, those developments that disregard environmental sustainability tend to degrade ecological capital and encourage pollution. This stark disparity typically arises from variations in EQ standards, workforce capabilities, and the capacity to adopt green technologies to adapt to market demand transitions—factors that further moderate the long-term impact of manufacturing on PP.

In Kukar, the MS and IC were positively and significantly associated with EQ, whereas LMP showed a negative but statistically insignificant association. In the PP equation, the MS and LMP were positively and significantly associated with PP, while IC and EQ did not show statistically significant associations. The interaction terms involving the MS and LMP with EQ showed positive and statistically significant associations with PP, whereas the interaction term involving IC was negative but not statistically significant at the 5% level. Regarding mediation, only the indirect association between LMP and PP through EQ was positive and statistically significant.

In terms of macroeconomic development, growth in the MS literally has a dual impact on EQ and PP. This is because manufacturing expansion boosts economic output, such as Gross Domestic Product (GDP), and generates employment, thereby increasing individuals’ incomes through wages and purchasing power. Paradoxically, manufacturing growth is also closely associated with substantial resource consumption due to high energy intensity, which can lead to increased emissions. A crisis in EQ arises when such growth is not accompanied by effective regulations and clean technologies. Evidence from 157 countries shows that intensive industrial development can exacerbate environmental impacts and pollution in the short term, despite the generally positive correlation with GDP [78].

Components of labour market absorption can diminish EQ because certain types of work—particularly those reliant on fossil fuels and energy-intensive processes—contribute to industrial waste and air pollution when work activity increases without the support of alternatives such as green technological innovations. In other practices, high IC often result from substantial investments in physical development, which can exacerbate environmental impacts if the infrastructure is not environmentally sustainable—for example, the use of fossil fuel-based materials in construction and transportation—thereby reducing EQ and significantly undermining prosperity. Using cross-country OECD panel data, Dechezleprêtre et al. [79] found that stricter environmental policies, accompanied by increased energy costs, have a significant negative impact on workers in energy-intensive MSs, even though these policies represent a novel approach to fostering clean innovation in other sectors.

Conditions in Asian countries exhibit a coherent structure. There is an interaction between industrialisation-driven economic growth and environmental regulation, with economic growth having complex and sometimes opposing effects on both economic output and EQ. Recently, a study by Li et al. [80], focusing on provinces in China, reported that increased environmental regulation can systematically promote the utilisation of ecological capital. Nonetheless, when such policy scenarios are driven by high-quality economic growth associated with industrialisation, the interaction between the two can sometimes suppress the development of ecological capital and hinder technological innovation due to the high compliance costs incurred by companies. Likewise, the situation in most Asian countries illustrates that investment in transport infrastructure within the framework of industrialisation does accelerate long-term economic growth in quantitative terms, but it also has the potential to increase pollution damage if not accompanied by stringent emission standards and the use of renewable energy sources. Consequently, these positive effects on economic output are accompanied by a negative impact on EQ. On the other hand, other literature on the effectiveness of environmental policies in OECD countries finds that the negative effects on the macroeconomy are relatively small in aggregate. These policies generate new uncertainties between those who are reliable and dominant in the industrial sector, which creates many jobs, and those who are in decline and reducing their dependence on the industrial sector. As a result, a gap has emerged: some countries are intensively promoting energy policies despite pressure from market demands, while the clean industry and service sectors are simultaneously benefiting [81].

sec.title: 6.1. Summary of findings
sec.p: This study adapts the multiple regression method into a moderated–mediation regression that not only traces the partial statistical associations of the MS, IC, and LMP on EQ, but also elaborates the impact of these four factors on PP. Also, the study employs EQ as a moderating or mediating variable in the relationships between these variables within the IKN, as reflected in PPU and Kukar over thirteen periods.

In summary, the empirical results validate several valuable findings, which can be divided into four points. First, in both PPU and Kukar, the MS is significantly associated with EQ; however, IC in Kukar are significantly related to EQ. Uniquely, the LMP in these two regions has no statistically significant association with EQ. Second, in PPU, IC were positively and significantly associated with PP, whereas this is not the case in Kukar. On the one hand, the MS in was not significantly associated with PP in PPU, but in Kukar, this sector plays a significant role in PP. LMP is significantly associated with PP in both regions. Third, the MS, when moderated by EQ, is an interaction term was positively and significantly associated with PP in both PPU and Kukar. Interestingly, in PPU, IC moderated by EQ have a clear statistically significant association with PP, but this is not observed in Kukar. A similar pattern is evident in the findings regarding LMP moderated by EQ on PP: the results are not significant in PPU but are significant in Kukar. Fourth, the results are also consistent for PPU and Kukar, as LMP showed a statistically significant indirect association through EQ on PP. An anomaly arises in other relationships, where the MS, mediated by EQ in both regions simultaneously, has no significant association with PP. In PPU, IC mediated by EQ showed a positive and significantly indirect association with PP, but this is not the case in Kukar. The findings of this study confirm that the success of the IKN area’s development is linked to not only by the expansion of economic activity, but also by the government’s ability to safeguard EQ, as EQ itself must be regarded as a key component in the formulation of regional development policy so that the economic benefits generated remain consistent with the principles of sustainability, particularly environmental resilience, on the long-term agenda.

sec.title: 6.2. Limitations and future research
sec.p: This study has several limitations that present opportunities for further refinement. Firstly, the scope of the analysis is confined to only two districts within the IKN region, limiting the generalisability of the findings to the entire IKN region or other regions in Indonesia. Secondly, the study relies exclusively on secondary data from government publications, which may involve inconsistencies in data collection instruments over time, limitations in accuracy, and an inability to capture the dynamics of public subjective perceptions regarding EQ and prosperity. Thirdly, the selection of independent variables remains narrow and primarily focused on structural economic aspects (manufacturing, infrastructure, and the labour market), thereby excluding institutional, social, governance, and other ecological dimensions such as climate change risks and biodiversity. Fourthly, although the adapted moderated--mediation regression model provides valuable insights into the relationships between the variables under consideration, the empirical findings should be interpreted as statistical associations rather than definitive causal effects. This study utilises observational secondary data at the regional level; consequently, it remains susceptible to issues of endogeneity, the possibility of reverse causality, bias arising from unobserved variables, and temporal heterogeneity. For instance, higher levels of community prosperity may increase a region’s fiscal capacity, strengthen environmental governance, and boost infrastructure investment, which in turn may also influence some of the explanatory variables in the model. In practice, the performance of the MS may be influenced by various other factors beyond the scope of the existing modelling analysis, such as government policy, natural resource-based economic activity, and investment dynamics. Future research could broaden the scope of study, employ more robust econometric techniques, incorporate additional or modify variables with diverse indicators, and integrate qualitative and quantitative data to develop a more comprehensive understanding.

Finally, the availability of IKLH data at the regency level—which has only been officially available since 2020—forms one of the main limitations of the present study. If the quantitative evaluation were to rely solely on this data source, the number of available observations would be significantly reduced, rendering it insufficient for a reliable analysis of the moderated-mediation regression model due to the resulting very limited degrees of freedom. Ideally, this study should utilise the full set of available annual data whilst transparently accounting for the treatment of IKLH data during periods when regency-level data was not yet available online. Meanwhile, the empirical findings need to be interpreted critically, taking into account these limitations in data availability. As the district-level IKLH data series becomes longer in future, it is hoped that subsequent research will be able to re-estimate the results using more up-to-date IKLH data to explore the robustness and consistency of the study’s findings.

sec.title: 6.3. Policy recommendations
sec.p: It should be noted that the test results confirm that EQ plays a key role in understanding the relationship between development activities and community prosperity in the IKN region. Empirically, policy priorities in PPU Regency need to be focused on strengthening the performance of the labour market and optimising infrastructure development, as these two pillars have been shown to have a significant impact on community prosperity, both directly and indirectly through EQ. EQ must be targeted as a supporting pillar so that the benefits of infrastructure and labour market development can be maximised to enhance community prosperity. Unlike PPU, Kukar Regency requires more intensive attention to strengthening the MS and the labour market, as these two sectors have been shown to have a more dominant relationship with both EQ and community prosperity. At this stage, industrial development policies need to be revitalised whilst safeguarding EQ, so that economic expansion remains managed in line with the sustainability of regional development. Beyond these empirical findings, the literature on sustainable development also highlights the urgency of a transition towards more environmentally friendly industrial practices, the implementation of adequate environmental standards, and the strengthening of environmental governance in infrastructure development. For the next phase, these recommendations are presented as conceptual policy pathways to ensure the sustainability of the IKN’s development.

Furthermore, differences in influence patterns between regions within the IKN highlight the need for policy autonomy tailored to local characteristics and contextual factors. In PPU, policy efforts should focus on optimising the labour market and infrastructure benefits by improving EQ as the primary means of supporting PP. Meanwhile, in Kukar, strengthening the synergy between the MS and the labour market through adaptive environmental regulations is a crucial step towards enhancing the economic impact on PP. Therefore, IKN policies should not be uniform but rather varied, emphasising a regionally based and integrated approach that addresses not only short-term and contemporary issues but also delivers long-term impacts to ensure competitive and inclusive development.
